label: PYQ-style
stem: When an electrolyte solution is diluted,
model_answer: **(b).** Fewer ions per unit volume, so $\kappa$ falls; ions from one mole are freer (or more of them, for weak electrolytes), so $\Lambda_m$ rises.

label: PYQ-style
stem: Define molar conductivity. With a sketch, show how it varies with $\sqrt c$ for a strong and a weak electrolyte.
model_answer: *How much to write: 3–4 lines + a labelled sketch · 4 minutes* **Molar conductivity** is the conductivity of a solution divided by its molar concentration: the conducting power of all the ions produced by one mole of electrolyte. $$\Lambda_m=\frac{1000\,\kappa}{M}$$ $$(\text{S cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1})$$ - **Strong electrolyte** (KCl): $\Lambda_m$ rises slowly and linearly on dilution, $\Lambda_m=\Lambda_m^\circ-A\sqrt c$, because ions move more freely. - **Weak electrolyte** ($\ce{CH3COOH}$): $\Lambda_m$ rises very steeply at low concentration because the degree of dissociation increases. :::tip Your answer must contain - the definition with "one mole of electrolyte" and the unit S cm² mol⁻¹ - a sketch with both axes labelled ($\Lambda_m$ against $\sqrt c$) and both curves named - the reason for each curve: ion mobility (strong), dissociation (weak) ::: **Marks are lost for:** plotting against c instead of √c; no labels on the curves; no unit.

scheme.step: Reason for strong and weak behaviour

hint: Conductivity divided by concentration. Strong: straight line; weak: steep curve near zero.

label: PYQ-style
stem: Write the anode, cathode and overall reactions of the lead storage battery during discharge. What happens to the density of the electrolyte?
model_answer:
*How much to write: four equations and one line · 4 minutes*

**Anode** (negative plate, oxidation):

$$\begin{aligned}&\ce{Pb(s) + SO4^2-(aq)}\\ &\quad\ce{-> PbSO4(s) + 2e-}\end{aligned}$$

**Cathode** (positive plate, reduction):

$$\begin{aligned}&\ce{PbO2 + SO4^2- + 4H+ + 2e-}\\ &\quad\ce{-> PbSO4 + 2H2O}\end{aligned}$$

**Overall:**

$$\begin{aligned}&\ce{Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4}\\ &\quad\ce{-> 2PbSO4 + 2H2O}\end{aligned}$$

The density of the electrolyte <mark>decreases</mark>, because <u>sulphuric acid is used up</u> and <u>water is formed</u>.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- both electrodes named with <u>oxidation</u> / <u>reduction</u>
- $\ce{PbSO4}$ formed at <mark>both</mark> electrodes
- balanced overall equation with $\ce{2H2SO4}$
- density <mark>decreases</mark>, with the reason
:::

**Marks are lost for:** writing the charging reactions; missing H⁺ or water at the cathode; "density increases".
hint: Lead is oxidised and lead dioxide is reduced; both end up as the same solid.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
Calculate the emf at 298 K of the cell
$\begin{gathered}\ce{Sn(s) | Sn^2+(0.004 M)}\\ \ce{|| H+(0.020 M)}\\ \ce{| H2(g, 1 bar) | Pt(s)}\end{gathered}$
Given $E^\circ_{\ce{Sn^2+/Sn}}=-0.14$ V.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 8–10 lines: cell reaction first, then Nernst · 6 minutes*

**Cell reaction:** $\begin{gathered}\ce{Sn(s) + 2H+(aq)}\\ \ce{-> Sn^2+(aq) + H2(g)}\end{gathered}$, so <mark>$n=2$</mark>

$$\begin{aligned}E^\circ_\text{cell}&=E^\circ_\text{cathode}-E^\circ_\text{anode} \\ &=0.00-(-0.14) \\ &=0.14\text{ V}\end{aligned}$$

**Nernst equation** (298 K):

$$E_\text{cell}=E^\circ_\text{cell}-\frac{0.059}{n}\log\frac{[\ce{Sn^2+}]}{[\ce{H+}]^2}$$

$$E_\text{cell}=0.14-\frac{0.059}{2}\log\frac{0.004}{(0.020)^2}$$

$$\begin{aligned}E_\text{cell}&=0.14-0.0295\log10 \\ &=0.14-0.0295\end{aligned}$$

$$\boxed{E_\text{cell}=0.11\text{ V}}$$

:::tip Your answer must contain
- the <u>balanced cell reaction</u>, which fixes $n=2$ and $Q$
- $E^\circ_\text{cell}$ as <u>cathode − anode</u>
- <mark>$[\ce{H+}]$ squared</mark> in $Q$ (solids and 1 bar $\ce{H2}$ left out)
- answer with unit V
:::

**Marks are lost for:** n taken as 1; [H⁺] not squared; Q written upside down.
hint: Write the cell reaction first. Q = [Sn²⁺]/[H⁺]² and n = 2.

label: PYQ-style
stem: A conductivity cell filled with 0.1 M KCl has resistance 100 $\Omega$. Filled with 0.02 M KCl it has resistance 520 $\Omega$. The conductivity of 0.1 M KCl is 1.29 S m$^{-1}$. Calculate the conductivity and molar conductivity of 0.02 M KCl.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 6–8 lines: cell constant first · 6 minutes* **Given:** 0.1 M KCl: $R=100\ \Omega$, $\kappa=1.29$ S m⁻¹; 0.02 M KCl: $R=520\ \Omega$
**To find:** $\kappa$ and $\Lambda_m$ of 0.02 M KCl **Step 1, cell constant** (same cell): $$\begin{aligned}G^*&=\kappa\times R \\ &=1.29\times100 \\ &=129\text{ m}^{-1}\end{aligned}$$ **Step 2, conductivity of 0.02 M KCl:** $$\begin{aligned}\kappa&=\frac{G^*}{R} \\ &=\frac{129}{520} \\ &=0.248\text{ S m}^{-1}\end{aligned}$$ $$\boxed{\kappa=2.48\times10^{-3}\text{ S cm}^{-1}}$$ **Step 3, molar conductivity:** $$\begin{aligned}\Lambda_m&=\frac{1000\,\kappa}{M} \\ &=\frac{1000\times2.48\times10^{-3}}{0.02}\end{aligned}$$ $$\boxed{\Lambda_m=124\text{ S cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1}}$$ :::tip Your answer must contain - the cell constant found from the standard KCl - unit conversion S m⁻¹ → S cm⁻¹ (÷ 100) before using 1000κ/M - two boxed answers with units ::: **Marks are lost for:** mixing S m⁻¹ with the 1000/M formula (answer 100 times too big); no cell constant step.
hint: Get the cell constant from the 0.1 M data: G* = κ × R. Convert S m⁻¹ to S cm⁻¹.

label: PYQ-style
stem: (a) State Kohlrausch's law. (b) $\Lambda^\circ_m$ for NaCl, HCl and CH$_3$COONa are 126.4, 425.9 and 91.0 S cm$^2$mol$^{-1}$. Find $\Lambda^\circ_m$ of CH$_3$COOH. (c) Why can't this value be found by extrapolating a graph?
model_answer:
*How much to write: law in two lines, the sum in three, reason in two · 6 minutes*

**(a) Kohlrausch's law:** <mark>the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the limiting molar conductivities of its cation and anion.</mark>

$$\Lambda_m^\circ=\nu_+\lambda_+^\circ+\nu_-\lambda_-^\circ$$

**(b)** Add and subtract so that only $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{CH3COO-}$ remain:

$$\begin{aligned}\Lambda^\circ_{\ce{CH3COOH}}&=\Lambda^\circ_{\ce{CH3COONa}}\\ &\quad+\Lambda^\circ_{\ce{HCl}}-\Lambda^\circ_{\ce{NaCl}}\end{aligned}$$

$$=91.0+425.9-126.4$$

$$\boxed{\Lambda^\circ_{\ce{CH3COOH}}=390.5\text{ S cm}^2\text{mol}^{-1}}$$

**(c)** For a <u>weak electrolyte</u>, $\Lambda_m$ rises <u>very steeply</u> at low concentration because dissociation keeps increasing, so the curve <mark>cannot be extrapolated</mark> to zero concentration.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- the words <u>limiting molar conductivity</u> and <u>sum of cation and anion contributions</u>
- the combination written in symbols before the numbers
- (c): <mark>steep rise / cannot be extrapolated</mark>
:::

**Marks are lost for:** adding all three values; stating the law without "limiting".
hint: Add and subtract the salts so that the unwanted ions cancel.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) For $\begin{gathered}\ce{2Fe^3+(aq) + 2I-(aq)}\\ \ce{-> 2Fe^2+(aq) + I2(s)}\end{gathered}$, $E^\circ_\text{cell}=0.236$ V at 298 K. Calculate $\Delta_rG^\circ$ and the equilibrium constant. (F = 96500 C mol$^{-1}$) [3]
(b) How many faradays are needed to deposit 1 mol of Al from molten $\ce{Al2O3}$? [1]
(c) Write the electrode reactions of the H$_2$–O$_2$ fuel cell. [1]
model_answer:
*How much to write: about one page: (a) in full, (b) and (c) in two lines each · 10 minutes* **(a) Given:** $E^\circ_\text{cell}=0.236$ V, $n=2$ (two electrons transferred), $F=96500$ C mol⁻¹ $$\begin{aligned}\Delta_rG^\circ&=-nFE^\circ_\text{cell} \\ &=-2\times96500\times0.236\end{aligned}$$ $$\Delta_rG^\circ=-45548\text{ J mol}^{-1}$$ $$\boxed{\Delta_rG^\circ=-45.55\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$ $$\begin{aligned}\log K_c&=\frac{nE^\circ_\text{cell}}{0.059} \\ &=\frac{2\times0.236}{0.059} \\ &=8.0\end{aligned}$$ $$\boxed{K_c=1\times10^{8}}$$ **(b)** $\ce{Al^3+ + 3e- -> Al}$, so 3 F are needed per mole of Al. **(c)** Fuel cell (alkaline electrolyte):
Anode: $\begin{gathered}\ce{2H2(g) + 4OH-(aq)}\\ \ce{-> 4H2O(l) + 4e-}\end{gathered}$
Cathode: $\begin{gathered}\ce{O2(g) + 2H2O(l) + 4e-}\\ \ce{-> 4OH-(aq)}\end{gathered}$ :::tip Your answer must contain - $n=2$ stated before using it - $\Delta G$ with unit and sign; $\log K_c$ formula written first - (b) the electrode equation showing 3 electrons - (c) reactions balanced with OH⁻ (alkaline medium) ::: **Marks are lost for:** n taken as 1; ΔG left in J without "mol⁻¹"; acidic fuel-cell equations.
hint: ΔG° = −nFE° with n = 2; then log K = nE°/0.059.

**Reason (R):** Zinc has a higher standard reduction potential than copper.

label: PYQ-style
stem: *An iron bridge near the sea needs repainting far more often than one inland. Rusting is not a simple reaction of iron with air: tiny electrochemical cells form on the wet metal surface. At one spot iron atoms give up electrons; these travel through the metal to another spot, where oxygen dissolved in the water film takes them up. Engineers slow the damage by coating the steel with zinc or by bolting blocks of magnesium to it.*

parts.stem: Write the reaction taking place at the anodic spot.
Why does iron rust faster near the sea?
parts.model_answer: Dissolved salts make the water film a better conductor (an electrolyte), so the electrochemical reactions go faster.

scheme.step: Dissolved salts make the water film a better conductor (an electrolyte), so the electrochemical reactions go faster.

parts.stem: Explain how a zinc coating protects iron even when it is scratched. What is the method of protection with magnesium blocks called?
parts.model_answer: Zinc has a lower reduction potential than iron, so zinc is oxidised in preference and iron stays as the cathode. Sacrificial protection (cathodic protection with a sacrificial anode).

scheme.step: Zinc has a lower reduction potential than iron, so zinc is oxidised in preference and iron stays as the cathode.
Sacrificial protection (cathodic protection with a sacrificial anode).

hint: Treat a rusting spot as a small galvanic cell: decide which metal is oxidised by comparing reduction potentials.
source_note: Added Nov 2026 (from the old case-based angles)
model_answer:
*How much to write: one line each for (i) and (ii); three lines for (iii) · 7 minutes*

**(i)** At the anodic spot iron is <u>oxidised</u>:

$$\ce{Fe(s) -> Fe^2+(aq) + 2e-}$$

**(ii)** Sea air carries <u>dissolved salts</u>, which make the water film a <mark>better electrolyte</mark>, so the electrochemical cells on the surface work faster.

**(iii)** Zinc has a <u>lower (more negative) reduction potential</u> than iron, so <mark>zinc is oxidised in preference</mark> and iron stays as the cathode, even where the coating is scratched. Bolting on magnesium blocks is called <mark>sacrificial (cathodic) protection</mark>.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- (i) the oxidation half-equation of <u>iron</u>
- (ii) the word <u>electrolyte</u> / conductivity
- (iii) <u>lower reduction potential</u> of zinc and the name <mark>sacrificial protection</mark>
:::

**Marks are lost for:** writing the cathode reaction for (i); saying zinc "covers" iron without the potential argument.

label: PYQ-style
stem: Calculate $\Delta_rG^\circ$ for the reaction $\begin{gathered}\ce{Zn(s) + Cu^2+(aq)}\\ \ce{-> Zn^2+(aq) + Cu(s)}\end{gathered}$, given $E^\circ_\text{cell}=1.10$ V. What does its sign tell you? (F = 96500 C mol$^{-1}$)
model_answer:
*How much to write: 4–5 lines · 4 minutes*

**Given:** $E^\circ_\text{cell}=1.10$ V; two electrons are transferred, so <mark>$n=2$</mark>

$$\begin{aligned}\Delta_rG^\circ&=-nFE^\circ_\text{cell} \\ &=-2\times96500\times1.10\end{aligned}$$

$$\Delta_rG^\circ=-212300\text{ J mol}^{-1}$$

$$\boxed{\Delta_rG^\circ=-212.3\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}}$$

The value is <u>negative</u>, so the reaction is <mark>spontaneous</mark>.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- <mark>$n=2$</mark> from the equation
- the formula $\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ$ before numbers
- unit kJ mol⁻¹ and the comment on the sign
:::

**Marks are lost for:** n taken as 1; answer in J without "mol⁻¹"; no comment on spontaneity.
hint: n is the number of electrons in the balanced cell reaction.

label: PYQ-style
stem: Write the reactions at the cathode and the anode when aqueous NaCl is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Why is sodium not deposited at the cathode?
model_answer:
*How much to write: two equations and one reason line · 4 minutes* **Cathode** (reduction): $\begin{gathered}\ce{2H2O(l) + 2e-}\\ \ce{-> H2(g) + 2OH-(aq)}\end{gathered}$
**Anode** (oxidation): $\ce{2Cl-(aq) -> Cl2(g) + 2e-}$ Sodium is not deposited because water has a higher reduction potential than $\ce{Na+}$: $E^\circ(\ce{H2O/H2})=-0.83$ V against $E^\circ(\ce{Na+/Na})=-2.71$ V, so water is reduced in preference. :::tip Your answer must contain - hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode - both potentials compared, or the words water is reduced in preference ::: **Marks are lost for:** writing Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na at the cathode; no potentials in the reason.
hint: Compare the reduction potentials of Na⁺ and water.

label: PYQ-style
stem: Calculate the emf at 298 K of the cell $\begin{gathered}\ce{Ni(s) | Ni^2+(0.01 M)}\\ \ce{|| Ag+(0.001 M) | Ag(s)}\end{gathered}$. Given $E^\circ_{\ce{Ni^2+/Ni}}=-0.25$ V and $E^\circ_{\ce{Ag+/Ag}}=+0.80$ V.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 8–10 lines: cell reaction first, it fixes n and Q · 6 minutes*

**Cell reaction:** $\ce{Ni + 2Ag+ -> Ni^2+ + 2Ag}$, so <mark>$n=2$</mark>

$$\begin{aligned}E^\circ_\text{cell}&=0.80-(-0.25) \\ &=1.05\text{ V}\end{aligned}$$

**Nernst equation** (298 K):

$$E_\text{cell}=E^\circ_\text{cell}-\frac{0.059}{2}\log\frac{[\ce{Ni^2+}]}{[\ce{Ag+}]^2}$$

$$E_\text{cell}=1.05-0.0295\log\frac{0.01}{(0.001)^2}$$

$$E_\text{cell}=1.05-0.0295\times4$$

$$\boxed{E_\text{cell}=0.932\text{ V}}$$

:::tip Your answer must contain
- the balanced cell reaction (two $\ce{Ag+}$ per Ni)
- <mark>$[\ce{Ag+}]$ squared</mark> in $Q$; $E^\circ$ of silver <u>not</u> doubled
- answer with unit V
:::

**Marks are lost for:** multiplying E°(Ag) by 2; forgetting the square; Q upside down.

scheme.step: Cell reaction, n = 2 and E°cell = 1.05 V

hint: Balance the electrons: two Ag⁺ for one Ni. The coefficient becomes a power in Q, not a multiplier on E°.

label: PYQ-style
stem: A current of 2.0 A is passed through copper sulphate solution for 40 minutes. Calculate the mass of copper deposited at the cathode. ($M_\text{Cu}=63.5$ g mol$^{-1}$, F = 96500 C mol$^{-1}$)
model_answer:
*How much to write: 6–8 lines · 6 minutes*

**Given:** $I=2.0$ A, $t=40$ min $=$ <u>2400 s</u>, $M_\text{Cu}=63.5$ g mol⁻¹

$$Q=I\,t=2.0\times2400=4800\text{ C}$$

At the cathode: $\ce{Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu}$, so <mark>2 F deposit 1 mol of Cu</mark>.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{mol of Cu}&=\frac{Q}{2F} \\ &=\frac{4800}{2\times96500} \\ &=0.0249\text{ mol}\end{aligned}$$

$$m=0.0249\times63.5$$

$$\boxed{m=1.58\text{ g}}$$

:::tip Your answer must contain
- time <mark>converted to seconds</mark>
- the electrode equation showing <u>two electrons</u>
- answer in grams
:::

**Marks are lost for:** time left in minutes; one electron per copper.
hint: Convert minutes to seconds; copper needs two electrons per atom.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
*City buses that run on hydrogen carry a fuel cell instead of an engine. Hydrogen and oxygen are fed continuously to porous carbon electrodes dipped in concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide, and the cell produces electricity, with water as the only product. Fuel cells convert about 70% of the energy of the fuel into electricity.*

*How much to write: one or two lines for each 1-mark part; full working for the 2-mark part · 7–8 minutes.*

parts.stem: Write the overall reaction in the fuel cell.
Give one reason why a fuel cell is more efficient than a thermal power plant.
parts.model_answer: It converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy, without first making heat, so less energy is wasted (about 70% against about 40%).

scheme.step: It converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy, without first making heat, so less energy is wasted (about 70% against about 40%).

parts.stem: Write the reactions at the anode and the cathode.

hint: The electrolyte is alkaline, so balance with OH⁻ and water. Where marks are lost: writing the reactions for an acidic electrolyte when the passage says NaOH.
model_answer:
*How much to write: one line each for (i) and (ii); two equations for (iii) · 7 minutes* **(i)** $\ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l)}$ **(ii)** A fuel cell turns chemical energy directly into electrical energy without first making heat, so less energy is wasted (about 70% against about 40% for a thermal plant). **(iii)** In alkaline electrolyte:
Anode: $\begin{gathered}\ce{2H2(g) + 4OH-(aq)}\\ \ce{-> 4H2O(l) + 4e-}\end{gathered}$
Cathode: $\begin{gathered}\ce{O2(g) + 2H2O(l) + 4e-}\\ \ce{-> 4OH-(aq)}\end{gathered}$ :::tip Your answer must contain - (ii) the word directly (no heat step) - (iii) equations balanced with OH⁻ and water ::: **Marks are lost for:** acidic equations when the passage says NaOH.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) Define limiting molar conductivity. Sketch and explain how molar conductivity varies with $\sqrt{c}$ for a strong and a weak electrolyte. [2]
(b) The molar conductivity of 0.0025 M ethanoic acid is 32.8 S cm$^2$mol$^{-1}$. Calculate its degree of dissociation and dissociation constant. Given $\lambda^\circ_{\ce{H+}}=349.6$ and $\lambda^\circ_{\ce{CH3COO-}}=40.9$ S cm$^2$mol$^{-1}$. [3]
model_answer: *How much to write: about one page: definition, sketch and reasons in (a); full working in (b) · 10–12 minutes* **(a)** **Limiting molar conductivity**, $\Lambda_m^\circ$, is the molar conductivity when the concentration approaches zero (infinite dilution). - Strong electrolyte: linear fall with $\sqrt c$; extrapolate to read $\Lambda_m^\circ$. - Weak electrolyte: steep rise at low $c$ as dissociation increases; cannot be extrapolated. **(b) Given:** $c=0.0025$ M, $\Lambda_m=32.8$ S cm² mol⁻¹ By Kohlrausch's law: $$\begin{aligned}\Lambda_m^\circ&=\lambda^\circ_{\ce{H+}}+\lambda^\circ_{\ce{CH3COO-}} \\ &=349.6+40.9 \\ &=390.5\end{aligned}$$ $$\begin{aligned}\alpha&=\frac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^\circ} \\ &=\frac{32.8}{390.5}\end{aligned}$$ $$\boxed{\alpha=0.084}$$ $$\begin{aligned}K_a&=\frac{c\alpha^2}{1-\alpha} \\ &=\frac{0.0025\times(0.084)^2}{1-0.084}\end{aligned}$$ $$\boxed{K_a=1.93\times10^{-5}}$$ :::tip Your answer must contain - the words concentration approaches zero - a labelled sketch of both curves - $\Lambda_m^\circ$ from Kohlrausch\'s law before α - $K_a$ formula written before numbers ::: **Marks are lost for:** unlabelled sketch; using Ka = cα² without saying it is approximate; dropping the unit of Λ.
hint: Get Λ°m from Kohlrausch, then α = Λm/Λ°m, then Ka.

label: PYQ-style
stem: A cell reaction has a standard EMF of 1.10 V and transfers 2 electrons. What is the standard Gibbs energy change for the cell reaction? (F = 96500 C mol$^{-1}$)
model_answer: **(B) −212 kJ mol$^{-1}$.** $\Delta_rG^\circ=-nFE^\circ_\text{cell}=-2\times96500\times1.10=-2.12\times10^{5}$ J mol$^{-1}$. A positive $E^\circ$ always gives a negative $\Delta_rG^\circ$. The −106 option uses n = 1.
